record.paper_title: Progress in Nuclear Astrophysics: a multi-disciplinary field with still many open questions
record.original_question: How can nuclear mass models for exotic neutron-rich nuclei be improved so that r-process calculations use masses and derived neutron-capture rates that remain accurate far from experimentally known nuclei? In the paper, current models can disagree by up to about ±5 MeV near important shell closures, causing neutron-capture rates to differ by 3 to 5 orders of magnitude, and the authors explicitly call for improved relativistic and non-relativistic mean-field models, beyond-mean-field corrections, and better treatment of odd-A and odd-odd nuclei together with broader agreement with other observables such as charge radii, neutron skins, fission barriers, spectroscopic data, nuclear-matter properties, and neutron-star properties.

evidence.quote: When considering mass models obtained in relatively different frameworks, e.g the Skyrme-HFB or Gogny-HFB mass models, deviations are also found in the mass predictions away from the experimentally known region. For example, as shown in Fig. 3, deviations up to typically ±5 MeV can be observed for exotic nuclei between HFB-31 [30], D1M [32] and BSkG2 [31], especially around the N = 126 and 184 shell closures. Neutron capture rates can consequently deviate by 3 to 5 orders of magnitude with such mass differences, essentially due to different local variations in the pairing and shell description. Such deviations by far exceeds what is acceptable for nucleosynthesis applications.

For this reason, further improvements of mass models are required. These include development of relativistic as well as non-relativistic mean field models, but also the inclusion within such approaches of the state-of-the-art beyond-mean-field corrections, like the quadrupole or octupole correlations by the Generator Coordinate Method [41, 42] and a proper treatment of odd-A and odd-odd nuclei with time-reversal

In addition to an accurate prediction of the known masses, such models should also aim for an accurate description of as many other (pseudo-)observables as possible. These include charge radii and neutron skin thicknesses, fission barriers and shape isomers, spectroscopic data such as the 2+ energies, moments of inertia, but also infinite (neutron and symmetric) nuclear matter properties obtained from realistic calculations as well as specific observed or empirical properties of NSs, like their maximum mass or mass-radius relations [43, 44].

artifact.category_tag: nuclear mass models for r-process nucleosynthesis
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a theoretical nuclear mass model capable of predicting atomic masses M(Z,N) of exotic neutron-rich nuclei (in particular near the neutron shell closures N = 126 and N = 184) with sufficient accuracy to be used in rapid neutron-capture (r-process) nucleosynthesis simulations. Concretely, construct a self-consistent mean-field (relativistic or non-relativistic, e.g. Skyrme-Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov, Gogny-HFB, or covariant density-functional) framework, augmented by beyond-mean-field corrections (such as quadrupole and octupole correlations obtained from the Generator Coordinate Method, and a proper treatment of odd-A and odd-odd nuclei including time-reversal symmetry breaking), such that:

1. The model reproduces all experimentally known atomic masses within current measurement uncertainties.
2. Predictions of unknown masses M(Z,N) for neutron-rich nuclei relevant to the r-process agree across independent parameterizations to substantially better than the current spread of approximately ±5 MeV near N = 126 and N = 184, so that the resulting (n,γ) neutron-capture rates (computed, e.g., via Hauser–Feshbach statistical theory using these masses as input) do not vary by the present 3–5 orders of magnitude between models.
3. The same model simultaneously reproduces, within accepted experimental error bars, additional nuclear (pseudo-)observables: charge radii, neutron-skin thicknesses, fission barriers and shape isomers, spectroscopic data such as 2⁺ excitation energies and moments of inertia, properties of infinite symmetric and pure neutron matter from ab initio calculations, and global neutron-star observables such as the maximum gravitational mass and the mass–radius relation.

Provide such a model (or prove its existence/non-existence under the constraints above) and quantify the residual uncertainty in r-process abundance predictions stemming from nuclear masses.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a long-standing open challenge in nuclear astrophysics. Recent literature (2023–2025) on mass models (BSkG3, relativistic DFT, machine-learning-augmented mass tables) continues to report mass deviations of several MeV for very neutron-rich nuclei near N=126 and N=184, with corresponding order-of-magnitude spreads in (n,γ) rates, indicating the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: BSkG3: Topical issue on nuclear mass models
status_evidence.snippet: New Skyrme-HFB mass model BSkG3 still shows several-MeV spreads with other global mass models for very neutron-rich nuclei.
status_evidence.claim: Mass-model disagreement persists for exotic neutron-rich nuclei.

status_evidence.title: Impact of nuclear masses on r-process abundances
status_evidence.snippet: Different mass models lead to large variations in r-process abundance patterns and neutron-capture rates near shell closures.
status_evidence.claim: r-process predictions remain sensitive to mass-model choice, problem unresolved.
